title: Routes, injections and vascular access
blurb: Give IM, subcutaneous and intradermal injections with the right angle and site, and give medicines safely through cannulas and enteral tubes.
question: A nurse is giving an intradermal tuberculin test into the inner forearm. Which sign shows the injection has been given correctly?

teach.body: The same drug can act very differently depending on the route: oral, sublingual, topical, inhaled, enteral (through a feeding tube), subcutaneous (SC), intramuscular (IM), intradermal (ID) or intravenous (IV). The prescription must state the route, and giving a medicine by a route other than the one prescribed is a medication error. Some wrong-route errors are so dangerous that they are Never Events, such as giving oral or enteral medicine or feed by any parenteral route.
teach.cite: RPS/RCN 2019 principle 15; NHS England Never Events list 2018 (updated 2021)

rows.label: Sign of success
values: Resistance and a raised blanched bleb

teach.caption: The Green Book says it is not necessary to aspirate after the needle enters the muscle. A 7 mm bleb is about 0.1 mL.

teach.caption: The buttock is avoided for vaccines because of sciatic nerve injury and the risk of injecting into fat. Two injections in one limb go at least 2.5 cm apart; record each site.

teach.body: For vaccinations, the Green Book advises that if skin is visibly clean, no further cleaning is necessary; only visibly dirty skin is washed with soap and water. For IV device insertion, skin is decontaminated with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol. Choose a needle long enough to reach the intended tissue: an intradermal injection uses a 26G, 10 mm (brown) needle. Needles and syringes are single use.
teach.cite: Green Book ch4; NICE CG139; NIPCM 1.5

teach.h: Giving an IV medicine through a cannula
items: Check the prescription, compatibility and rate; prepare with ANTT.
Clean the port with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol and let it dry.
Flush with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride to confirm patency; stop if pain, swelling or resistance.
Give the drug at the prescribed rate, observing the person and the site.
Flush again, clean the port, dispose of sharps at the point of use and record.

teach.caption: CG32: check NG tube position after placement and before each use. CG139: flush before and after feeds or medicines.

teach.body: Oral liquid medicines are measured and given with approved oral or enteral (ENFit) syringes that cannot connect to IV catheters or ports, never with IV syringes. This NPSA barrier exists to prevent the Never Event of giving oral or enteral medication by a parenteral route. For enteral tubes, flush with freshly drawn tap water, or cooled boiled or sterile water if the person is immunosuppressed (CG139).
teach.cite: NPSA alert 2007 (in NHS England Never Events recommendations); NICE CG139 1.3.4.2

Clear labelling of bags and syringes
teach.caption: Never Events are wholly preventable because strong national barriers exist; they are reported on LFPSE.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Leila and Mr Osei
teach.body: Leila gives Mr Osei, 45, his influenza vaccine. His deltoid skin is clean, so she does not swab it. She stretches the skin and inserts the needle at 90°, does not aspirate, and records the site. Later she gives his IV antibiotic: she cleans the port, flushes with 0.9% sodium chloride, gives the drug over the prescribed time and flushes again. When his liquid paracetamol is due, she uses an oral syringe, not an IV syringe.

teach.text: Angles: IM 90° (skin stretched), deep SC 45° (skin bunched), ID almost parallel with a bleb. A common error is bunching the skin for IM or stretching it for SC: it is the other way round.

items: IM 90° skin stretched; deep SC 45° skin bunched; ID bevel up, resistance and a raised bleb.
Vaccines: deltoid or anterolateral thigh (thigh for infants under 1); avoid the buttock; no need to aspirate.
IV: clean the port, flush with 0.9% sodium chloride before and after, observe the site.
NG tube: confirm position (pH 5.5 or below) before each use; flush before and after medicines.
Oral liquids in oral/enteral syringes, never IV syringes; wrong-route oral to IV is a Never Event.

summary: You can now choose the angle, skin technique and site for IM, SC and intradermal injections and recognise a correct intradermal bleb. You can also give medicines safely via a cannula and an enteral tube, keeping oral and IV routes apart.

A.q: An occupational health nurse gives an intradermal tuberculin test into the inner forearm of Leila, 24. Which finding confirms the injection has been given correctly?
options: A small pale bleb forms, raising the skin at the site
The fluid flows in easily with no resistance felt
A small bead of blood appears when the needle is removed
The skin is bunched up around the needle during injection
A.why: The Green Book describes considerable resistance and a raised, blanched bleb as signs of a correct intradermal injection.

whyNot.1: No resistance suggests the injection is too deep; the needle should be removed and reinserted.
whyNot.2: Bleeding is not a sign of a correct intradermal injection.
whyNot.3: For intradermal injection the skin is stretched, not bunched.

A.q: Oliver, 38, is to have an intramuscular vaccine into his deltoid. At what angle should the needle be inserted?
options: 15°, almost parallel to the skin
45°, with the skin bunched up
30°, with the bevel facing down
90°, with the skin stretched
A.why: Green Book ch4: IM injections are given with the needle at 90° to the skin, with the skin stretched, not bunched.

whyNot.0: Almost parallel is the intradermal technique.
whyNot.1: 45° with bunched skin is the deep subcutaneous technique.
whyNot.2: 30° is not a recognised IM angle and would place the drug too shallow.

A.q: Which site is preferred for an intramuscular vaccine in a 6-month-old baby?
options: The upper outer buttock
The deltoid of the upper arm
The anterolateral thigh
The abdomen around the umbilicus
A.why: The anterolateral aspect of the thigh is preferred for infants under 1 year because it provides a large muscle mass (Green Book ch4).

whyNot.0: The buttock is avoided for vaccines because of sciatic nerve risk and injecting into fat.
whyNot.1: The deltoid is used for older children and adults; in infants the muscle mass is small.
whyNot.3: The abdomen is a subcutaneous site for some medicines, not an IM vaccine site.

B.q: Yusuf, 50, is prescribed co-amoxiclav 1.2 g by slow IV injection over 3 to 4 minutes via his cannula. The second check is complete. What is the correct sequence?
options: Give it over 30 seconds and then flush the cannula
Flush with water for injections, then give it as a rapid push
Give it over 3 to 4 minutes without flushing, to avoid fluid overload
Flush to confirm patency, give over 3 to 4 minutes, flush again
B.why: Patency is checked with a 0.9% sodium chloride flush, the drug is given at the prescribed rate, and the line is flushed again (CG139 1.4.4).

whyNot.0: Giving faster than prescribed risks adverse effects.
whyNot.1: Sterile 0.9% sodium chloride is the preferred flush, and a rapid push breaches the prescribed rate.
whyNot.2: Without a flush, patency is unchecked and drug remains in the cannula.

B.q: Pauline, 67, has a fine-bore nasogastric tube after a stroke. Her morning medicines are due through the tube. The tube was confirmed in position on insertion yesterday. What must the nurse do first?
options: Give the medicines, as position was confirmed yesterday
Inject air and listen over the stomach for a whoosh
Test an aspirate and confirm a pH of 5.5 or below
Check that the external tube length looks about right
B.why: NICE CG32 requires NG tube position to be checked after placement and before each use, with an aspirate pH of 5.5 or below (X-ray if needed).

whyNot.0: A tube can move after placement; position is checked before each use.
whyNot.1: The 'whoosh test' is not a safe method of confirming position.
whyNot.3: External length helps spot movement but does not confirm the tip is in the stomach.

B.q: A nurse needs to measure 5 mL of oral paracetamol suspension. The only syringes on the trolley are IV Luer syringes. What should she do?
options: Obtain an oral or enteral syringe before measuring the dose
Use an IV syringe and label it clearly as an oral medicine syringe
Pour it into a cup by estimating 5 mL by eye
Use an IV syringe and remove the needle first
B.why: Oral liquid medicines are measured and given with approved oral/enteral syringes that cannot connect to IV devices, preventing the Never Event of oral medicine given by a parenteral route.

whyNot.1: Labelling does not stop an IV syringe connecting to an IV line.
whyNot.3: Removing the needle does not stop a Luer syringe connecting to a cannula.

C.q: Eric, 58, has a PEG tube. Paracetamol suspension and baclofen liquid are due at 12:00 while his feed is running. He is not immunosuppressed. How should the nurse give them?
options: Mix both liquids into the feed bag so that they run in slowly with it
Give them through the feed line without stopping the pump
Give both together in one syringe without flushing the tube
Stop the feed, flush with tap water, give each medicine, flush after
C.why: CG139 advises flushing before and after medicines with freshly drawn tap water for people who are not immunosuppressed. Medicines are not mixed into the feed.

whyNot.0: Adding medicines to feed risks interactions, blockage and inaccurate dosing.
whyNot.1: Medicines are not given while feed is running through the same line.
whyNot.2: Mixing medicines and skipping flushes risks blockage and interactions.

C.q: Grace, 72, needs two vaccines today in the same arm because her other arm has lymphoedema. How far apart should they be given?
options: At least 1 cm apart
At least 5 cm apart
At least 2.5 cm apart
At the same site, one after the other
C.why: Green Book ch4: if more than one injection is given in the same limb, they should be at least 2.5 cm apart, with each site recorded.

whyNot.0: 1 cm is closer than the Green Book recommends.
whyNot.1: 5 cm is more than required; 2.5 cm is the minimum stated.
whyNot.3: Giving both at one site makes reactions impossible to attribute.

C.q: A nurse is about to give a vaccine into Mr Hart's deltoid. His skin is visibly clean. A student asks whether she should first wipe the site with an alcohol swab. What is the best answer?
options: Yes, a swab is required to sterilise the site
No, clean skin needs no further cleaning before vaccination
Yes, but use chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol instead
No, but she should wash the site with soap and water beforehand
C.why: The Green Book advises that if skin is clean, no further cleaning is necessary; disinfecting makes no difference to complication rates. Visibly dirty skin is washed with soap and water.

whyNot.0: Swabbing does not sterilise the skin and is not required for vaccination.
whyNot.2: Chlorhexidine in alcohol is for IV device insertion, not routine vaccination.
whyNot.3: Washing is for visibly dirty skin only.

reteach.title: Depth decides the technique
reteach.question: How deep do you want the medicine to go: skin, fat or muscle?

blocks.body: Intradermal goes just into the skin, so the needle lies almost flat and you see a bleb. Subcutaneous goes into the fat, so you lift a fold (bunch the skin) and go in at 45°. Intramuscular goes through the fat into muscle, so you stretch the skin flat and go straight in at 90°. The deeper the target, the steeper the angle.

blocks.text: IM: stretch the skin. SC: bunch the skin. Mixing these up places the drug in the wrong tissue.

explain.body: 90°, skin stretched, deltoid or anterolateral thigh for vaccines (thigh in infants), avoid the buttock, no need to aspirate.

test.q: What does the Green Book advise about aspirating after inserting an IM vaccine needle?
options: Aspirate for 5 seconds before injecting
Aspirate twice at different depths
Aspirate and inject if no blood appears
It is not necessary to aspirate
test.why: Green Book ch4: it is not necessary to aspirate the syringe after the needle is introduced into the muscle.

whyNot.0: Routine aspiration is not advised in the Green Book.
whyNot.2: This describes a traditional practice the Green Book does not require.

explain.body: Deep SC injections at 45° with the skin bunched; used for some vaccines, and for vaccines normally given IM in people with bleeding disorders.

test.q: Mr Ford has haemophilia and needs a vaccine normally given IM. How does the Green Book advise giving it?
options: By deep subcutaneous injection
By IM injection with a longer needle
By intradermal injection
By IV injection over 2 minutes
test.why: For individuals with a bleeding disorder, vaccines normally given IM should be given by deep subcutaneous injection to reduce the risk of bleeding.

whyNot.1: A longer IM needle increases the risk of a muscle haematoma.
whyNot.2: Intradermal is a different route not used as a substitute here.

explain.body: 26G, 10 mm brown needle, bevel up, about 2 mm into the dermis, almost parallel; resistance and a raised blanched bleb confirm placement.

test.q: During an intradermal injection, no resistance is felt and no bleb forms. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue, as this means the whole dose is going in correctly
Remove the needle and reinsert before giving more
Inject faster to raise a bleb
Massage the site to spread the fluid
test.why: If no resistance is felt, the needle should be removed and reinserted before more is given (Green Book ch4).

whyNot.0: No resistance suggests the needle is too deep.
whyNot.2: Injecting faster does not correct a needle that is too deep.
whyNot.3: Massage does not correct the depth of injection.

explain.body: IV: clean port, flush with 0.9% sodium chloride before and after. Enteral: confirm NG position before each use, flush with water before and after, oral/enteral syringes only.

test.q: What should be used to flush the enteral tube of a person who is immunosuppressed?
options: Cooled boiled water or sterile water
Freshly drawn tap water
Sterile 0.9% sodium chloride
Carbonated water to help clear any blockages
test.why: CG139 1.3.4.2: cooled freshly boiled water or sterile water from a freshly opened container for people who are immunosuppressed.

whyNot.1: Tap water is for people who are not immunosuppressed.
whyNot.2: 0.9% sodium chloride is the IV flush, not the enteral one.
whyNot.3: Carbonated drinks are not recommended flushes.
